chapter: Early memories on St. Philip Street
title: George Lewis's riverfront dock job and El Morocco
summary: Her father worked the riverfront by day and nights, and returned to it in 1952 when El Morocco closed a week after the move.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: What about, what are your memories of George at that time? Or what, was he working on the dock stand?

Yeah, yeah. Uh, he worked there in the daytime and he worked, uh, at night. I don't know if it was every night during that time, but I remember him very well. He worked there every day. Uh, cause I can remember him trying to work on his bicycle. Uh, when he'd come home in the evening, I'd be sitting outside the front door waiting for him. And I can remember him paddling down the street on his red and white bicycle. On his what? Red and white bicycle. Yeah. But, uh, I know he was working at night, but I don't know if it was regular work at night. But the riverfront, I remember very well.
Did he go down to the riverfront every day? Oh, yes. So you sort of had a regular job? Yeah, that was regular.
Because even after we moved over here in 52, he went back on the riverfront.
Oh, he did that, didn't he? Oh, yeah. After 52?
Yeah. Because, uh, I think it was a week after we moved over here, uh, El Morocco closed down and he just went back on the riverfront. Oh, really?
Uh-huh. He was playing at El Morocco his latest, that was it? Uh-huh. Can you remember, can you by any chance remember the month when you moved over here?
